deposition_export.note: global means of the central influx (the smoke arrives after years, mostly at high latitudes; the map's diurnal pattern averages out)

influx.note: Total mass of interplanetary dust and small meteoroids entering the atmosphere. Published estimates range from about 5 to 300 t/day (e.g. radar, lidar, spacecraft and ice-core methods); 30-100 t/day is the commonly quoted range.

limitations: the total influx is a scenario input: published estimates range from about 5 to 300 t/day; the Gruen distribution sets only the shape

single-body entry of homogeneous spheres on straight paths: no fragmentation, no differential evaporation of elements, no porous or icy particles; the vapour pressure is calibrated to the micrometeorite collections
the water content of the dust (hydrated minerals, solar-wind rims) is uncertain by a factor of a few
meteoric smoke is a burden estimate (residence time x ablation), not a transport model; its optical properties and the sign of its forcing are uncertain
point sources on the sky stand for the sporadic meteoroid environment; meteor showers, the velocity of each source and the gravitational focusing by latitude are left out
the comparison quantities (hydrogen escape, volcanic water, aeolian iron, ...) are rounded literature orders of magnitude

map.land_mask_source: global-land-mask 1.0.0 (MIT; GLOBE 1 km elevation, NOAA), sampled at the cell centres by tools/make_land_mask.py

comparisons.note: Rounded literature orders of magnitude: hydrogen escape ~3 kg/s, helium ~50 g/s; oceans 1.4e21 kg; precipitation ~5e17 kg/yr; volcanic and hydrothermal water ~1 Gt/yr; iron in aeolian dust deposition ~16 Mt/yr; geothermal heat flow ~47 TW; climate feedback 1.13 W/m2/K as in the solar model.
